title: Early modern philosophy I: Descartes and the rationalists
audience: a college student in a philosophy degree program, or an adult studying the same material on their own
purpose: Read Descartes, Spinoza and Leibniz on method, certainty, God, substance, mind and body, and freedom and necessity, together with Descartes's critics and correspondents (including Elisabeth of Bohemia) and Malebranche on causation, using modernized versions of the texts.
primary_reading: Early Modern Texts: free modernized versions of the classic texts

weeks.1: The scientific revolution and the new philosophy
weeks.3: Descartes: the cogito and clear and distinct ideas
weeks.4: Descartes: the proofs of God and the Cartesian circle
weeks.5: Descartes: mind, body and the real distinction
weeks.6: Elisabeth of Bohemia and the problem of interaction
weeks.11: Leibniz: the principle of sufficient reason and the best possible world
weeks.12: Leibniz: the identity of indiscernibles and the nature of space

blocks.deliverable: Explain the three stages of doubt in the First Meditation.
Reconstruct one proof of God and the circle objection.
Write out Elisabeth's objection and the strongest reply.
Week 7 midterm; reconstruct Spinoza's argument that there is only one substance.
Compare Spinoza and Leibniz on mind and body.
Evaluate the principle of sufficient reason in two pages.
Submit the project; take an unseen 120 minute final in week 14.

project: Rationalist systems essay: in 2,000 words, compare how Descartes, Spinoza and Leibniz answer one question (how many substances there are, how mind and body are related, or whether everything happens of necessity), reconstruct the central argument of each, and defend the view you find strongest against one objection.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
